# The Mean Gradient Is Not the Regime {#c13}

<span class="thread">SG · Sub-Gaussian safe zone · LG · Landscape and update geometry</span>

<span class="lens-ledger">Geometric supporting · Dynamic primary · Algorithmic supporting</span>

At $w=1$, the scalar loss $f(w)=w^2/2$ has gradient one. Take the update
$w^+=w-0.5g$, where $g=1+\xi$ is conditionally unbiased. If
$\E[\xi^2]=0.25$, then $\E[f(w^+)]=0.15625$: expected descent from the
initial loss $0.5$. If $\E[\xi^2]=4$, then $\E[f(w^+)]=0.625$: expected
ascent. The current state, mean gradient, curvature, and step size are
identical. Only the conditional dispersion changed.

::: {.callout-important title="Prediction"}
An optimizer plot reports a mean gradient norm but not the estimator's
conditional variance or tail behavior. Can it identify whether step decay or
batch growth is the relevant intervention? No: it has not identified the
regime.
:::

## Declare the estimator before its variance {#sec-c13-estimator}

Let $\mathcal F_k$ contain everything known before sampling at step $k$. A
usable stochastic-gradient contract is

$$
\E[\vect g_k\mid\mathcal F_k]=\nabla f(\vect w_k),\qquad
\E[\|\vect g_k-\nabla f(\vect w_k)\|^2\mid\mathcal F_k]
\leq \sigma_k^2.
$$ {#eq-c13-estimator}

The conditioning matters. Sampling without replacement, correlated examples,
adaptive data selection, clipping, and quantization can all alter the mean or
dispersion. “Gradient noise” without a filtration, averaging rule, and target
is not yet a mathematical object.

::: {#thm-c13-conditional-descent phenomenon_id="c13-mean-not-regime"}
### Conditional expected descent

Suppose $f$ is $L$-smooth and @eq-c13-estimator holds with finite conditional
second moment. For $\vect w_{k+1}=\vect w_k-\alpha\vect g_k$,

$$
\E[f(\vect w_{k+1})\mid\mathcal F_k]
\leq f(\vect w_k)-\alpha\left(1-\frac{L\alpha}{2}\right)
\|\nabla f(\vect w_k)\|^2+\frac{L\alpha^2}{2}\sigma_k^2.
$$ {#eq-c13-descent}
:::

### Proof

Apply the smoothness upper bound to $-\alpha\vect g_k$, condition on
$\mathcal F_k$, and use
$\E\|\vect g_k\|^2=\|\nabla f(\vect w_k)\|^2+
\E\|\vect g_k-\nabla f(\vect w_k)\|^2$.

When the variance bound is tight, the right side predicts descent whenever

$$
\alpha < \frac{2/L}{1+\sigma_k^2/\|\nabla f(\vect w_k)\|^2}.
$$ {#eq-c13-safe-step}

The ratio $\chi_k=\sigma_k^2/\|\nabla f(\vect w_k)\|^2$ is the diagnostic
axis. Small $\chi_k$ is gradient-dominated; large $\chi_k$ is noise-dominated.
This is an internal regime ledger, not a fifth narrative sigil.

    scalar_quadratic_regime(1.0, 0.5, ratio).expected_next_loss
    for ratio in ratios

axis.axhline(
    0.5, color="#b33a3a", linestyle="--", label="starting loss"
)
axis.scatter(
    [0.25, 4.0], [0.15625, 0.625], color="#d98c10", zorder=3
)
axis.set(
    xlabel=r"conditional noise-to-signal ratio $\chi_k$",
    ylabel="expected next loss",
)
axis.legend(frameon=False)
fig.tight_layout()
# [4]
assert np.isclose(conditional_safe_step(1.0, 4.0, 1.0), 0.4)

assert claim["harness_wheel_sha256"] == wheel_digest
assert claim["result"]["high_noise"]["expected_next_loss"] == 0.625

## Batch size is an assumption-bearing lever {#sec-c13-batch}

For a mean of $b$ conditionally independent, identically distributed
per-example estimators with finite variance, the variance becomes
$\sigma_k^2/b$. Then @eq-c13-safe-step explains the linear-scaling heuristic
only in the noise-dominated range: multiplying batch and step by the same
factor approximately preserves the variance penalty while that factor is
small enough that the smoothness term remains benign. Correlation, changing
data distributions, or infinite variance break the derivation.

The inequality also explains why “decrease the step” and “increase the batch”
can address the same term while having different compute and communication
costs. C01's traffic contract must therefore accompany the statistical one.

## Clipping repairs a tail by changing the target {#sec-c13-clipping}

Let $g=-9$ with probability $0.1$ and $g=19/9$ otherwise. Its mean is one and
variance is $100/9$. Clipping to $[-2,2]$ lowers variance to $1.44$ but moves
the mean to $1.6$. The estimator is no longer unbiased for the original
gradient. This is the C06 lesson inside an update: variance reduction and
target preservation are separate audit columns.

::: {.callout-warning title="Named wrong answer: clipping makes the theorem apply"}
Clipping supplies bounded tails for the clipped estimator. It does not make
that estimator unbiased for the unclipped gradient. A convergence argument
must carry the bias term or redefine the objective it targets.
:::

## Acceleration is a branch, not a survey {#sec-c13-acceleration}

On an exact positive-definite quadratic, momentum transforms each fixed
eigenmode into a second-order recurrence. Its stable region and accelerated
Chebyshev rate can be derived from that control problem. Once curvature moves
and stochastic forcing enters, the same memory can amplify noise. We retain
the exact quadratic as a calibration exercise and defer method variants: the
trunk question is which resolution the theory uses—global, local,
direction-aware, or finite-horizon—and which regime the evidence probes.

## Check yourself {#sec-c13-check}

With $L=1$, gradient norm two, and conditional variance 12, the noise-to-signal
ratio is three and @eq-c13-safe-step gives $\alpha<0.5$. Averaging four
independent copies reduces the ratio to $0.75$ and raises the threshold to
$8/7$. Neither conclusion survives without the independence and finite-second-
moment clauses.

## Sources and further reading {#sec-c13-sources}

The conditional descent calculation is standard in large-scale stochastic
optimization; see @bottou2018 and the foundational approximation scheme of
@robbins1951. Heavy-tailed gradient evidence is discussed by @simsekli2019.
The 2026 ICML tutorial by Mark Schmidt supplied the intellectual map from
theory resolution to regime diagnosis; the equations and qualifications here
are derived on the page rather than attributed to the tutorial.
